newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - China's army is business dynamite.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China's army is business dynamite.

text.p: China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) has evolved into the mainland's biggest conglomerate over the past 10 years and is spreading overseas, a leading expert says.

Cheung Tai Ming said it has tentacles in every domestic money-making sector -- agriculture, industrial manufacturing and service industries -- and is heading abroad, notably into Hong Kong, North America, the former Soviet Union and Southeast Asia.
Cheung, who is planning a book on the PLA's emergence as a major business powerhouse, said about one third of the hotels in China's southern province of Guangzhou are owned by the PLA.
In telecommunications, it is partners with U.S. multinationals like AT&T, Motorola and Unisys, focusing on pagers, mobile telephones and infrastructure construction, he said.
Cheung said the PLA accounts for about 10 percent of the Chinese medicine produced in China and owns four of the top 10 textile companies.
According to Chinese figures, the PLA's declared profit in 1993 was US$1 billion on a turnover of US$6-9 billion. Cheung said he believes real profits are at least double that.
MILITARY FORCES SEEN AS PLA INC
In a recent visit to Singapore, Cheung, a Hong Kong-based China expert at Kim Eng Securities, called it PLA Inc.
He said at a conference and in an interview it had an output equivalent to about three percent of China's gross domestic product and owned about 200 of China's largest industrial enterprises.
The PLA has 50 conglomerates -- huge enterprises with subsidiaries in many countries -- and about five to eight new ones are sprouting every year, he said.
PLA Inc comprises 15,000-20,000 companies, but it is the 10 percent, or 1,000 to 2,000, of these companies which are making waves in the international markets, Cheung said.
These are medium to large scale companies with assets of several hundred million dollars and which employ tens of thousands of people.
"PLA is one of China's most powerful institutions -- politically, ideologically, in terms of policy making and increasingly, economically," Cheung said.
When Deng Xiaoping came to power, economic development became top priority in the early 1980s.
"The government could no longer afford the high defense investments. Deng began to cut back defense budget. The military began to go into business," Cheung said.
TIGHT BUDGET FORCES MOVE INTO BUSINESS
The massive arms cuts in 1985 forced PLA arms factories and farms into business, fuelling an unchecked, free-wheeling growth in the commercial and service industries in 1993.
"For example, in 1979, there were 50 companies involved in the service industry belonging to the PLA. 10 years later, there were 5,000," Cheung said.
At the end of 1995, there was a shift in gear among PLA units towards quality and healthy integrated growth.
Cheung cited the history of China Poly Group, the PLA's largest conglomerate as an example of the evolution of PLA Inc.

Set up in 1984, China Poly was originally involved in the arms trade, but by 1992, it had changed its role and identity and began focussing on property and finance, domestically and overseas, with offices in the United States, Macau, Burma, Russia and Thailand, he said.
These companies are run by China's princelings -- children of China's top cadres, Cheung said.

At the apex is the Communist Party -- the Central Military Commission. Overall control of China's military business complex is vested in the army's gneral logistics department, which controls the PLA's purse strings.

Agriculture accounts for seven to eight percent of the total turnover of PLA Inc, while industrial manufacturing like printing and chemicals contribute 45-50 percent of PLA's turnover and 45 percent of profits, Cheung said.
Service industries contribute 45-50 of turnover and 50-55 percent of profits, he said.
FOREIGN FIRMS PURSUE PLA AS PARTNER
Foreign companies have pursued the advantages of a partnership with the PLA to get a foothold in the world's most populated country with more than one billion people.
The PLA enjoys tax subsidies, a good distribution and network channels. Cheung said its power and connections makes it immune to civilian oversight.
"Many civilian companies will not want to supervise the PLA companies because they are so powerful," Cheung said.
But he said these advantages could weigh on PLA Inc.
"They are conservatively managed and running along the military line makes them inflexible to market trends," he said.
"They also have heavy financial burdens as a lot of the profits are given back to officials. This offsets any subsidies they enjoy."

Corruption is also on the rise. Hundreds of PLA "shell" companies, firms incorporated with just HK$1.00, have mushroomed in Hong Kong and tax havens like British Virgin Islands and Cayman Islands, he said.
Undeclared profits are moved to these havens to escape strict audit or repossession by authorities, resulting in smuggling, misuse of state funds and subsidies, he alleged.
